articles.title: DR Congo: Ebola disease survivors share their stories
articles.description: Christine and her ten-year-old son, Jérémie, fell sick with Ebola disease after attending a funeral in September. “Soon after getting home, I started to get headaches,” says Christine. “The next day, it got worse.” The pair visited a local hospital, but as their symptoms – vomiting and diarrhoea – got worse, they were eventually transferred to the Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) Ebola treatment centre (ETC) in Beni, North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Medical staff feared they would not make it. In the more than six months since the Ebola disease outbreak was declared in DRC, close to 12,000 people have been infected, according to the Ministry of Health. The true figure is certainly higher. Around half of the people who are infected die from the disease. One of the reasons that the mortality rate is so high is that many people seek care only when the disease has already reached an advanced stage. “We can do more to increase the chances of survival of patients who come as soon as they experience symptoms,” says Dr Louis Vala Moweni, medical coordinator for MSF’s Ebola response. “But many arrive too late.” Ebola disease can progress rapidly and lead to severe complications. This is why patients should seek medical care as soon as they develop early symptoms, such as fever and headaches. Although the outbreak was officially declared in May, many people still hesitate to come to ETCs because of fear, misinformation, and distrust towards the Ebola response. “I thought that no one makes it out of here alive and that doctors and nurses kill people,” says Ghislaine, another survivor recently discharged from the Beni ETC. “I was surprised to experience the opposite.” For Dr Moweni, high levels of fear in the community are understandable. “At the beginning of the outbreak, people saw medical staff arriving in full personal protective equipment (PPE) and taking patients away,” he says. “Regrettably, many people died. We need to acknowledge that this instils fear in communities.” However, thanks to their testimonies, survivors are now helping to counter rumours and strengthen communities’ trust in health teams. “Seeing survivors walk out of ETCs alive, and hearing what they have to say is one of the best ways to combat that fear,” says Dr Moweni. In Mongbwalu, Ituri province, where the outbreak originated, there were significant fears when we began our response in May. “People were dying in cascades,” recalls Deogracias Kasereka, a pastor from the town, who later fell ill after presiding over a funeral. His daughter, who had worked on a previous outbreak, encouraged him to get tested for Ebola disease. “At that time, people were afraid, because going to the hospital meant death,” says Pastor Kasereka. “But I made up my mind. I said to myself, ‘if I must die of Ebola, then I will die. And if I can be cured, then I will be cured’. So, I decided to go.” After testing positive, the pastor was treated at the ETC and, in June, became the first patient in the town to recover from Ebola disease. Patients started to arrive at earlier stages of infection and mortality rates among them began to fall. “When they saw me alive, it encouraged many people,” he says. “They had said, ‘Even the pastor will die’. But seeing me return gave people hope.” “From the day I was discharged, I began awareness-raising in the community,” says Pastor Kasereka. “I went directly into the church communities to speak to people. Since then, I have continued this work, even in schools.” While attitudes towards the response are changing in some areas, some survivors still face acute stigma. “There is often a paradox in the experience of survivors,” says Dr Moweni. “While they want to put their experience to the benefit of their communities and contribute to the fight against the outbreak, they can also become victims of stigma and attacks. This adds to their suffering at a time when they are still recovering from the disease.” When Francine, who fell ill with Ebola disease after losing one of her children to the disease, was discharged from the Mongbwalu ETC in October, she found that the community had burned down her home — fearing it to be contaminated. “I do not want to speak with them anymore,” says Francine. “I do not know how I will survive.” At a survivor clinic supported by MSF, and adjacent to Mongbwalu ETC, patients receive medical and psychological support through individual consultations. MSF pays for transport costs to help survivors living far away reach the clinic. “Some survivors are feared in their communities,” says Jean-Paul Wayotho Pariu, an MSF health promoter. “We advise them how to reintegrate and how to avoid shame and feel at ease. The perception of this disease makes many people see it as shameful.” Despite the challenges, patients who survive Ebola disease also feel great relief. “I am happy to return home,” says Christine, on the day of her release, alongside Jérémie, after more than a month of treatment. “In the ETC, I spent the whole time thinking about my family and my children.” Her message to the community is clear: “If other people feel sick, they should come to the ETC and not stay at home. They [healthcare staff] will look after you.”

articles.title: I’m not interested in having sex with near strangers. As a newly single man, how do I navigate dating? | Leading questions
articles.description: You don’t have to have sex because it’s ‘what’s expected’, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. But you may want to be explicit about what you do want Read more Leading questions How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”). I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. I’ve always been into the person, not just the body, but it takes time to get to know someone enough to feel comfortable being intimate. So how can I keep a nice relationship going, so that I can develop the trust I need for sex, without them losing interest because I’m not doing (what I assume) everyone else on the dating scene is doing? Continue reading...

articles.title: Healthcare Triangle Stock Plunges After Hours: What's Happening?
WHO Director-General's opening remarks at joint media briefing with the Ministry of Public Health, Haiti – 25 November 2026
articles.description: Minister Sinal, Minister Forbin, Members of the ambassadors, my colleagues from the UN, press, and friends, Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us today. First, I would like to sincerely thank Minister Sinal and the Government of Haiti for their warm welcome and for the constructive discussions we have had during my visit. It has given me the chance to reaffirm WHO/PAHO's solidarity with Haiti and its people, including my personal commitment for WHO to do all in its power to support the country. During my visit earlier today to Hôpital Universitaire La Paix here in the capital, Port-au-Prince, I saw first-hand the strain the facility and its staff are working under, and the patients and families waiting for care. It moved me. Haiti's health system is under serious strain from the high volume of patients and the influx of trauma cases. Armed violence, widespread displacement and disease outbreaks add to the pressure on an already fragile system. In 2026, an estimated 4.9 million people need health assistance. Behind every number is a mother, a child, a family. Health facilities have been forced to close, and too many families are unable to access even the most basic health services. As you know, H.U.P. is the last major public referral hospital still operating in Port-au-Prince, a city where only 38% of health facilities are fully functional. Across Haiti, a country of more than 11 million people, only a quarter (24.5%) of health facilities are fully functioning. Since January of this year, with support from WHO/PAHO, H.U.P. has managed to treat more than 19 575 emergency patients, including 291 victims of gunshot wounds, perform 3086 surgeries, and handle 1442 high-risk deliveries. From my heart, I thank the brave, committed and talented health workers who provide a lifeline for the people of Port-au-Prince. They are working day and night in one of the most challenging humanitarian and health crises globally, and they continue to show great courage and dedication. I was proud to meet some of them earlier today. I also want to recognize the leadership of Minister Sinal and the Ministry of Public Health and Population in sustaining essential health services under difficult circumstances. Earlier today, I met with the Prime Minister. I left that meeting encouraged and inspired by what the government is doing with the limited resources it has, especially with maternal and child health at the center. His message to the international community was, I quote: “We will do our best, and you support us based on the priorities we set for our country.” It is a message we should listen to. Through our Regional Office for the Americas, PAHO, WHO is working closely with the Ministry and our partners to support emergency medical care, respond to outbreaks, strengthen disease surveillance and immunization, and maintain access to essential medicines and medical supplies. Even so, Haiti’s Ministry of Public Health and Population has moved forward with the introduction of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine to help prevent cervical cancer. Our discussions have reaffirmed three shared priorities. First, protecting health workers, patients and health facilities. Second, ensuring safe and sustained access to essential health services. And third, strengthening Haiti's health system to respond not only to today's emergencies, but also to tomorrow's challenges. Health is not only a humanitarian priority. Health is a fundamental human right, and a foundation for peace, stability and sustainable development. These efforts require strong national leadership, sustained international solidarity and predictable financing. I want to thank our partners for their continued support, which is helping to save lives every day. But the needs remain significant. The people of Haiti need our support today, and our partnership in the years ahead. They are not alone. Minister Sinal, You can count on WHO and PAHO's continued solidarity, commitment and support. I can say this on behalf of the whole UN family. We stand with you, and with the people of Haiti. Thank you. Merci. Mèsi anpil.
